The White mullet Mugil curema attains an ultimate total length of 91 centimeters in both sexes, representing a substantial terminal body size characteristic of this coastal mugilid. Field surveys conducted along the Atlantic coast of Florida have consistently documented females reaching 91 cm [Li = 91 cm], and males achieve an equivalent terminal length of 91 cm [Li = 91 cm], indicating negligible sexual size dimorphism in this mugilid. The total length at puberty is considerably smaller, with individuals typically attaining sexual maturity at 19.7 cm [Lp = 19.7 cm], indicating that the onset of gonadal activity occurs at roughly one-fifth of the maximum length. This early reproductive onset is ecologically advantageous for a species subject to variable juvenile recruitment, allowing a substantial portion of the population to contribute to the spawning stock before experiencing the elevated mortality risks associated with larger body sizes in estuarine environments. The length-weight relationship for this species follows an allometric scaling exponent near three, reflecting isometric growth in body mass relative to length.

Reproductive output in M. curema is considerable, particularly under the warm thermal conditions typical of its subtropical spawning grounds. When maintained at a water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], females produce approximately 10,959 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 10,959 eggs per day], a rate sustained by continuous batch spawning over an extended reproductive season. This daily fecundity estimate, derived from gonadal examinations of gravid females, positions M. curema among the more fecund iteroparous teleosts of its body size. The high daily reproductive rate reflects a strategy of compensatory spawning in response to substantial egg and larval mortality in coastal planktonic environments. The temperature dependency of this process is critical; at this water temperature, metabolic rates are sufficiently elevated to support the energetic demands of continuous oocyte production and vitellogenesis, whereas cooler conditions would substantially suppress reproductive output. Field observations confirm that spawning aggregations are most dense when surface water temperatures approximate this thermal optimum, linking reproductive phenology directly to the region's seasonal warming cycle.

Egg size in M. curema is modest, with a mean diameter of 0.9 millimeters reported for congeneric Mugil cephalus, a value presumed similar for this species given the close phylogenetic relationship. Based on an egg diameter of 0.9 mm, the calculated wet weight of a single fertilized ovum is 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams], placing M. curema at the smaller end of the pelagic egg size spectrum among marine teleosts. This small egg size is consistent with a high-fecundity life-history strategy, wherein individual offspring receive minimal maternal investment per unit, favoring numerical abundance over per-capita provisioning. The transparent, yolk-laden eggs drift within the upper water column for a brief incubation period before chorion rupture releases a lecithotrophic larva that depends entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves for several days. The initial wet mass of the egg thus sets a fundamental constraint on early larval survival, limiting the duration of the endotrophic phase before the onset of exogenous feeding must occur to prevent starvation mortality.

Adult body mass in M. curema scales predictably with the ultimate lengths recorded for each sex, reaching substantial maximum values. Females attain an ultimate wet weight of 7,220 grams [Wwi = 7,220 grams], a mass that reflects the accumulation of somatic tissue and gonadal products over their lifespan. Males achieve a comparable maximum body mass of 7,220 grams [Wwi = 7,220 grams], indicating that the absence of length dimorphism is paralleled by equivalent mass trajectories between the sexes. These values place M. curema among the larger members of its genus, comparable to the well-studied Mugil cephalus in terms of asymptotic size. At puberty, individuals weigh approximately 77.9 grams [Wwp = approximately 77.9 grams], a threshold representing only about one percent of the ultimate adult mass. This early weight-at-maturity implies that energetic investment switches rapidly toward reproductive structures while substantial somatic growth continues, a pattern of indeterminate growth common in subtropical estuarine fishes. The length-weight scaling in M. curema adheres closely to a cubic relationship, typical of species with isometric growth in body depth.

Longevity in M. curema is moderate for a fish of its asymptotic size. At a water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum lifespan reaches approximately 8,395 days [am = approximately 8,395 days]. This value, equating to roughly 23 years, positions the species as relatively long-lived within the Mugilidae, exceeding the typical 10-to-15-year maxima reported for many tropical mugilids. The long lifespan is ecologically consistent with a schooling, iteroparous life history that depends on repeated spawning events across multiple seasons to buffer against recruitment failures in unpredictable coastal habitats. At this temperature, the metabolic costs of sustained activity remain manageable, allowing individuals to partition energy effectively between growth and reproduction over several decades. Age determination from otolith annuli confirms that few individuals exceed this maximum age in the wild, with natural mortality rates increasing sharply after approximately 20 years due to senescent decline in physiological condition and increased susceptibility to predation. The relatively extended lifespan ensures multiple reproductive opportunities, a critical demographic hedge in variable environments.
